title: Comprehension

toc.title: 4.1 Comprehension of reading passages: General and Technical English

html:
Comprehension carries about 4 of the 16 English questions (our estimate) and mixes General English and Technical English passages.

In the official model paper one passage with a Section B question (2 marks) is printed: a passage on how English words label animals, with the question "In the English language the animals are used for unpleasant comparisons".

Passage questions are the most learnable English marks: there is no unseen rule, only a method.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • The main idea / purpose of the passage and the best title.
  • A fact stated directly (scan the text) versus a conclusion that has to be inferred.
  • The meaning of a word or phrase in context.
  • The writer's tone and attitude; what is not mentioned (NOT / EXCEPT).
  • Technical passages: define, compare, cause and effect, sequence of a process.

4.1 Comprehension of reading passages: General and Technical English

Method for a two-minute passage

  1. Read the questions first (not the options) so you know what to look for.
  2. Read the passage once for the main idea; underline the first and last sentences of paragraphs, which usually state the argument and its conclusion.
  3. For each question, find the sentence in the passage that answers it; do not answer from memory or from outside knowledge. Eliminate options that are true but not stated, too extreme (always, never, only, all), or opposite.
  4. Vocabulary-in-context: replace the word with each option and see which keeps the sentence meaning.
  5. Inference: the answer must follow necessarily from the text; the passage does not need to say it in the same words.
  6. Tone words: critical, objective, optimistic, ironic, sympathetic, cautionary.

Time: at most 2 minutes per Section B question; a long passage at 2 marks is a quick mark once you have the method.

Question types, in order of difficulty

Type How to answer
detail ("According to the passage…") locate and match the text
main idea / title cover every paragraph, not one detail
vocabulary in context substitute and test
inference ("It can be inferred…") the one option that must be true
purpose / tone what the writer is doing: warning, explaining, persuading
NOT / EXCEPT find the three true statements; the fourth is the answer

Technical English passages

They explain a device, a process, a material, a safety rule or a measurement.

Expect: definitions (is defined as), classification (two types), process sequence (first, then, finally), cause and effect (as a result, because), comparison (whereas, unlike), numerical data.

Read the numbers carefully; one option often reverses a comparison (higher versus lower).

Practice passages

Passage 1 — General English

Cities have always been shaped by the way people move. The earliest towns were small enough to cross on foot, so shops, homes and workplaces stood close together.

When the railway arrived, towns stretched along the tracks, and when the car became common, they spread out into wide suburbs that most people could only reach by driving.

Planners now see the cost: long commutes, polluted air and roads so crowded that new lanes fill up within a few years of opening. Several cities have therefore begun to reverse the trend.

They are building cycle lanes, protecting pavements and encouraging homes, offices and markets to share the same neighbourhoods.

Early results suggest that such changes do not slow business; shops on pedestrian streets often report more customers, not fewer.

The lesson is not that cars should disappear, but that a city designed around the car alone leaves many of its residents worse off.

Questions

  1. The passage is mainly aboutahow transport has shaped cities and why some now change coursebthe history of the railwaycthe dangers of cyclingdthe economics of car manufacturing
  2. According to the passage, early towns had homes and workplaces close together becausealand was cheapbthere were no carscpeople travelled on footdplanners ordered it
  3. The word "reverse" in the passage most nearly meansacopybturn backcacceleratedignore
  4. Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a cost of car-based planning?along commutesbpolluted airccrowded roadsdhigher rents
  5. The writer would most likely agree thatacars should be banned from citiesbpedestrian streets harm local tradeca city built only for cars disadvantages many residentsdrailways caused the suburbs
Answers and explanations — Passage 1

1. (a) — the passage traces transport and its effect on city shape, then describes the change of direction.

2. (c) — "small enough to cross on foot".

3. (b) — "reverse the trend" means turn it back.

4. (d) — long commutes, polluted air and crowded roads are named; rents are not.

5. (c) — the last sentence says exactly this;(a) is explicitly rejected ("not that cars should disappear"),(b) is contradicted.

Passage 2 — Technical English

A transformer changes the voltage of an alternating current without changing its frequency. It consists of two coils of insulated wire, the primary and the secondary, wound on a common core made of thin laminated sheets of soft iron.

When an alternating voltage is applied to the primary, it produces a changing magnetic flux in the core, and this flux induces a voltage in the secondary.

The ratio of the voltages is equal to the ratio of the number of turns in the two coils. A step-up transformer has more turns in the secondary and raises the voltage, whereas a step-down transformer does the opposite.

Because the power cannot increase, a rise in voltage is always accompanied by a fall in current.

This is why electricity is sent over long distances at very high voltage: the smaller current wastes less energy as heat in the transmission lines.

The core is laminated, not solid, to reduce the eddy currents that would otherwise heat it.

Questions

  1. A transformer does NOT changeathe voltagebthe currentcthe magnetic flux in the coredthe frequency
  2. In a step-up transformerathe secondary has more turns than the primarybthe primary has more turns than the secondarycboth coils have equal turnsdthe current rises
  3. Power is transmitted at high voltage becauseathe current is smaller, so less heat is lost in the wiresbthe frequency becomes lowercthe eddy currents are reduceddthe wires become thinner
  4. The core is laminated in order toaincrease the voltagebreduce eddy currentscraise the frequencydinsulate the coils
  5. The word "accompanied" in the passage is closest in meaning toaprecededbreplacedcoccurring together withdprevented by
Answers and explanations — Passage 2

1. (d) — the first sentence: "without changing its frequency".

2. (a) — "A step-up transformer has more turns in the secondary".

3. (a) — "the smaller current wastes less energy as heat".

4. (b) — stated in the last sentence.

5. (c) — "a rise in voltage is always accompanied by a fall in current" means they occur together.

Passage 3 — General English (inference and tone)

Many students believe that the best way to learn is to read the same chapter several times. The comfortable feeling of familiarity is, however, easily mistaken for understanding.

Researchers who compare study habits repeatedly find that students who close the book and try to recall what they have read remember far more a week later than those who simply reread.

Testing yourself is harder and feels less productive in the moment, which is precisely why many learners avoid it. The wise student treats difficulty not as a sign of failure but as evidence that the memory is being strengthened.

Questions

  1. The writer's attitude toward rereading is best described asaenthusiasticbmildly criticalchostiledindifferent
  2. "precisely why" in the passage suggests that the difficulty of self-testingais a reason students skip itbproves it is uselesscmakes it fundis exaggerated
  3. Which can be inferred from the passage?aFamiliarity can give a false sense of knowingbRereading never helpscSelf-testing is easydResearchers prefer rereading
  4. The best title for the passage isaThe Joy of ReadingbA History of Study MethodscWhy Recall Beats RereadingdHow to Write an Exam
Answers and explanations — Passage 3

1. (b) — it questions rereading without attacking it ("easily mistaken for understanding").

2. (a) — learners avoid self-testing because it is hard.

3. (a) — "familiarity is easily mistaken for understanding".

4. (c) — the passage compares recall with rereading.

Formula and fact sheet

Step Action
1 read the questions first
2 read once for the main idea
3 match each answer to a sentence
4 eliminate extreme or unstated options
5 test vocabulary by substitution

Chapter summary

  • Read the questions first; answer only from the passage.
  • The best title and main idea cover the whole passage.
  • Vocabulary questions are settled by context.
  • Technical passages: watch for numbers, definitions and cause–effect links.
  • NOT/EXCEPT questions: three options are in the text, the fourth is not.

Practice questions

Set A — Recall (6 questions)

  1. In the passage on city transport, the writer says that new road lanesanever fill upbcost nothingcare always cycle lanesdfill up within a few years
  2. In the passage on transformers, the primary and the secondary areatwo coils of insulated wirebtwo coresctwo currentsdtwo frequencies
  3. According to the passage on study habits, students who test themselvesaforget fasterbremember more after a weekcread more oftendfeel more comfortable
  4. A step-down transformerahas more turns in the secondarybraises the voltagechas fewer turns in the secondarydraises the power
  5. In the transport passage, shops on pedestrian streets often reportafewer customersbno changechigher pricesdmore customers
  6. The core of a transformer is made ofalaminated sheets of soft ironba solid copper blockcinsulating plasticdsteel wire
Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (d) — "new lanes fill up within a few years of opening".

2. (a) — "two coils of insulated wire, the primary and the secondary".

3. (b) — "remember far more a week later".

4. (c) — it does the opposite of step-up.

5. (d) — "more customers, not fewer".

6. (a) — "thin laminated sheets of soft iron".

Set B — Understanding (5 questions)

Read the passage below and answer the questions.

Nepal gets nearly all of its electricity from rivers, because steep mountains and monsoon rain give its rivers great energy. In the dry winter, however, the flow falls and some plants produce much less power.

Engineers therefore build reservoirs that store water in the wet season, and they also connect the grid to India so that surplus power can be sold in summer and shortfalls covered in winter.

  1. The main idea of the passage isaNepal has no electricity problemsbIndia produces power for Nepalchydropower is Nepal's main source, with seasonal limits that engineers managedthe monsoon damages power plants
  2. The word "shortfalls" most nearly meansasurplusesbdeficitscprofitsdfloods
  3. Reservoirs help because theyastore wet-season water for the dry seasonbincrease rainfallccool the riversdreduce the slope
  4. The passage implies that in summer Nepal often hasasurplus powerbtoo little powercno riversda broken grid
  5. Which is NOT mentioned as a way of handling the dry-season problem?areservoirsbthe grid link with Indiacsolar farmsdselling surplus in summer
Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (c) — hydropower, winter low flow, reservoirs and the grid link.

2. (b) — shortfalls are deficits.

3. (a) — "store water in the wet season".

4. (a) — "surplus power can be sold in summer".

5. (c) — solar farms are not mentioned.

Group D — Model answers for long questions (10 marks each, for deeper revision)

  1. Read a technical passage and answer questions on its main idea, vocabulary in context, inference and reference, giving reasons. [10]
  2. Explain a method for reading a passage under time pressure and answering true/false, inference and tone questions. [10]

Model answer D1: A technical passage worked in full (10 marks)

Passage (about 120 words). A solar water heater has three main parts: a collector, an insulated tank and connecting pipes. The collector is a flat box with a black metal plate under a sheet of glass. Sunlight passes through the glass and heats the plate, and the glass traps the heat inside, just as a closed car becomes hot in the sun. Water in the tubes fixed to the plate becomes warm and, being lighter, rises to the tank by natural circulation, while cold water sinks to take its place. No pump is needed. In Nepal such heaters are popular in hotels and homes, because they reduce the use of electricity and firewood. However, they work poorly on cloudy days, so many users keep an electric heater as a back-up.

Questions and model answers.

  1. Main idea: (c) A solar heater uses sunlight to warm water, with a few limits. The passage explains the parts, the working, the use and the weakness. The wrong options cover only one part each.
  2. Vocabulary: "insulated" means covered to stop heat escaping. The clue is that the tank keeps the water warm.
  3. Reference: "they" in "because they reduce the use of electricity and firewood" refers to such heaters (solar water heaters), the plural noun that the sentence just named.
  4. Inference: Why do many users keep an electric heater? Because the solar heater gives too little heat on cloudy days. The word "however" signals the limit, and "back-up" tells us the reason.
  5. True or false: "A pump is needed to move the water." False. The passage says "No pump is needed" because natural circulation moves the water.
  6. Comparison: The glass is compared to a closed car in sunlight, which shows that glass traps heat.
  7. Tone: The writer's tone is informative and balanced, as it gives both a benefit and a drawback without strong emotion.
  8. Title: "How a Solar Water Heater Works."

Technique used. The answers come from the exact words of the passage, not from outside knowledge, and a wrong option usually contains a word that the passage never says or that changes its meaning ("always", "only", "never").

Question type Where to look Warning
Main idea First and last sentences Avoid options that cover only one detail
Vocabulary in context Words around the term Do not use the first meaning that comes to mind
Reference The noun just before the pronoun Check singular and plural
Inference Signal words (however, therefore) Must be supported by the text
True/False The exact sentence Beware of only, always, never

Conclusion. Every answer must be traced to a sentence in the passage; this removes guessing and saves time.

Model answer D2: Reading strategy under time pressure (10 marks)

Introduction. The English paper has about 4 comprehension questions, and a long passage can use up the time of the whole section. A fixed method makes the reading fast and accurate.

Method (8 steps).

  1. Read the questions first (not the options), so that you know what to look for.
  2. Skim the passage in about 30 seconds: the title, the first sentence of each paragraph and the last sentence.
  3. Read the passage once at normal speed, marking names, numbers and signal words (but, however, therefore, although).
  4. Answer the main-idea question last, because the details will have made the main idea clear.
  5. Find each answer in the text and underline the proof sentence before choosing an option.
  6. Remove wrong options: an option that is too general, too extreme, or true in real life but not in the passage is wrong.
  7. For vocabulary, replace the word with each option and check the sentence still makes sense.
  8. For tone and attitude questions, look at adjectives and verbs: praise, criticise, warn, explain.

Example of eliminating options. The passage says: "Most Nepali farmers still depend on the monsoon for irrigation." The question: Which statement is true? (a) All farmers use machines. (b) Most farmers depend on rain.

(c) Rain never falls in Nepal. (d) The monsoon is useless. Option (a) is extreme (all), (c) is extreme (never), (d) contradicts the text, so the answer is (b).

Time plan. A 150-word passage and 4 questions in about 4 minutes: 30 seconds for questions, 90 seconds for reading, 120 seconds for the answers. Practice passages in this chapter average 152, 165 and 99 words, so this plan fits.

Step Time Result
Questions and skim 40 s Know what to find
Careful reading 90 s Marked text
Answers with proof 110 s Four checked answers

Conclusion. A short, repeatable routine of reading the questions, skimming, locating proof and eliminating options turns comprehension into a safe scoring section.
